title: A nonprofit reports that more than 80 influencers on X were likely paid to promote articles favouring Nvidia and two AI-industry groups
standing: A nonprofit founded in 2024 by Tyler Johnston that publishes investigations of AI companies. Its site lists no funders; SFF's 2024 round recommended $31,000 to it from Jaan Tallinn (see its record).
claim: over 80 different influencers on X have likely been paid to endorse and link
source: The Midas Project, “Who paid right-wing influencers to promote Nvidia chip sales to China?”, 16 Nov 2026
why: It names two AI-industry groups as beneficiaries, one of them tied to a super PAC on this map, in the same weeks as the claims about funded journalism.

checks.what: The groups it names: “Build American AI is a dark-money group tied to pro-AI super PAC Leading the Future.” and “Innovation Council Action, a dark-money group linked to Trump AI Advisor David Sacks.” It gives the campaigns to Urban Legend, “an influencer marketing company”, and shows one influencer's “#ad #BuildAmericanAI”. These are the claimant's findings, not a check of them.
checks.source: The Midas Project, 16 Nov 2026

checks.what: A Cybernews report on the same campaigns (“80+ influencers paid to promote Nvidia sales in China”).
checks.source: Cybernews

responses.who: Urban Legend, as reported by the Midas Project
responses.what: “Urban Legend declined to comment.”

responses.who: Build American AI, Innovation Council Action and NVIDIA, as reported by the Midas Project
responses.what: “did not respond to requests for comment.”

open: Who paid for each campaign. The article: “there doesn't appear to be a single funder that paid for all of them”, and “it's likely that the full extent of such campaigns — and who is funding them — will remain unknown”.
cautions: The article says itself: “There's no conclusive link between Nvidia and these campaigns.” And: “Urban Legend doesn't disclose publicly who pays for a particular campaign, so it's hard to know for sure.”
“Likely” is the article's word: the payments are inferred from tracking links and disclosures on some posts.

This record was gathered and worded with AI models made by Anthropic, and Anthropic stands near both sides: NVIDIA committed in November 2025 to invest up to $10 billion in it (see NVIDIA), and Coefficient Giving and the Survival and Flourishing Fund, which fund Tarbell and others on this thread, are tied to it through people and money shown on their records. standing: A nonprofit founded in 2024 by Tyler Johnston that publishes investigations of AI companies. Its site lists no funders; SFF's 2024 round recommended $31,000 to it from Jaan Tallinn (see its record).

title: Posts on X call the coverage of Jensen Huang a coordinated campaign, citing a chatbot's table of reporters' ties to an AI-journalism nonprofit
claimed_by: An X user (a private person, not named here), posting a screenshot of a ChatGPT answer
standing: A reader of the coverage, not a party to it. The table was written by an AI chatbot in answer to a prompt that asked for “the recent hit pieces on Jensen Huang” and their links “to the EA movement”.
claim: Holy shit man, this is an insanely coordinated campaign. This is way worse than what I expected to learn
source: post on X, read on a screenshot given to this project
why: It joins a funding record that can be checked at its source (the Tarbell Center's donors, fellows and grants) to an inference of coordination, and the step between the two can be read.

checks.what: The table's donor lines (Coefficient Giving, Survival and Flourishing Fund and Longview Philanthropy at $1M+; EA Infrastructure Fund and Future of Life Institute at $100K–$1M). Tarbell's own supporters list, “grouped by lifetime giving”, shows the same names in the same bands.
checks.source: Tarbell Center for AI Journalism, About

checks.what: The table's $10 million program and its two grants. Tarbell's release of 5 Oct 2026: “The first two grantees under this program are NPR’s Power and Influence team and Machine Gods.” It gives Machine Gods “a grant of $480,000”; its grants page gives NPR's team “a grant of $250,000”.
checks.source: Tarbell Center for AI Journalism, blog, 5 Oct 2026

checks.what: The table's “His publication is operated by Tarbell”, of Transformer. Tarbell: “Tarbell is the publisher of Transformer, a publication covering the power and politics of transformative AI.” The same page: “Transformer retains full editorial independence from Tarbell”.

checks.what: The table's origin line: “Tarbell originated as a project of Training for Good. Its organizers advertised it on the EA Forum in 2022 and subsequently described their objective as placing people into journalism and policy careers that reduce risks from advanced AI.” The 2022 post lists the “Tarbell Fellowship (journalism)” for journalists covering topics “such as global poverty, animal welfare, and existential risks”, and says Training for Good “runs fellowships that place talented professionals in impactful careers in policy, journalism & other areas.” The AI-risk wording comes in the 2023 post: “Journalism as a career path is neglected by those interested in reducing risks from advanced AI.” The table's one sentence joins the two.

checks.what: Coordination: any page, among those the table cites and those read for this record, saying that coverage of Huang was coordinated, assigned or directed by Tarbell or its donors. None was found. Tarbell's fellowship page: “The specific assignments Tarbell Fellows pursue are up to our partner newsrooms and their editors.” Semafor (4 Oct 2026): “Semafor has not found instances where Tarbell interfered directly in any stories”.

title: An outlet reports that an Anthropic employee manages a consensual-non-consent party business, and that women in AI feel pressured to attend
claim: The orgies have been the subject of sexual assault allegations and sparked debate about the AI industry's attitudes toward women, some of whom report feeling pressured to attend the orgies in order to advance their careers.

checks.what: Business filing: the 17 Aug 2023 statement of information for Red Means No LLC lists three managers, one of them the Anthropic employee named in the article.
checks.source: California Secretary of State filing, via bizprofile.net

checks.what: “Runs a business”: a March 2026 registry snapshot still lists him as one of two managers. A manager listing does not say who runs the events; the article's own body says he is “listed as a manager”.
checks.source: bizprofile.net registry page

checks.what: The business's rules: its site says its events are “designed to be spaces to both ignore the "nos" of others, and have your own "nos" ignored”, that “By entering and wearing a wristband, you give default consent to all the actions listed”, including “Moderate Spanking”, “Wrestling” and “Light pain (1–5/10)”, with “Light electricity” and “Moderate beatings*” “permitted with negotiation”. The same site says consent is revocable with the word “red”, that “actual consent violations are strictly forbidden”, that entry is by application, and that attendees sign a consent form and waiver. No public complaint process is described.
checks.source: the business's own website (named, not linked)

checks.what: An assault account: a first-person post (24 Feb 2025, the last of a three-part series) describes her first Red Means No party: a participant “ignored the default consent rules, fucking multiple women without protection”. She calls it “a form of sexual assault”, writes that she was “actually sexually assaulted at my first CNC party”, and calls him “the stealther”. It says the organizers “kicked the stealther out of the party, made him submit additional follow-up STI tests”, “banned him from future parties, and reported the incident to other party organizers in the area”, and “wrote up an in depth incident report”. The post does not say whether the incident was reported to the police. It also says “The support I received from my new poly community was revelatory.” No account of another incident was found.
checks.source: the author's own post on Substack (a private person, not named here); the Free Beacon article links to it

checks.what: Career pressure: the article gives it to unnamed women and critics, and quotes three named commentators (below). The post it quotes says “There are some who are contesting the assertion that it functions as an AI networking event”. A third party's post on X shown there quotes the researcher as “I personally do upgrade my assessment of someone's AI alignment qualifications if I find out they go to [Red Means No]” (his own comment reads “absolutely do upgrade”) and “there are many other signals which can substitute for it.”
checks.source: Ivy Astrix, Substack, 1 Oct 2026

checks.what: The cofounder's own account (Feb 2023): she started the parties after “wishing someone would just come over and take me despite my complete lack of enthusiasm”; the ideal ratio is “about 2:3 women to men”; ignoring a partner's STI preferences “would result in expulsion from the event.”
checks.source: Aella, Substack, 8 Feb 2023

checks.what: A post on X (17 May 2024) by an AI researcher who says she never worked for OpenAI, opening “To the journalists contacting me about the AGI consensual non-consensual (cnc) sex parties”: “I don't think events like the consensual non-consensual (cnc) sex parties … have been good for women”; they are “emblematic of broader problems: a coercive climate that normalizes recklessness and crossing boundaries”. She writes there is “nothing wrong imo with sex parties and heavy LSD use in theory, but combined with the shadow of 100B+ interest groups, leads to some of the most coercive and fucked up social dynamics that I have ever seen.”

checks.what: The researcher's original comment (30 Sep 2026): “I personally absolutely do upgrade my assessment of someone's AI alignment qualifications if I find out they go to RMN”, calling it “one of many possible strong signals that someone can dismiss mainstream stupidity” and adding “there are many other signals which can substitute for it.” He also wrote “I have been to RMN more than once, and I think it is mostly rationalists actually. But it's close enough to 50/50 that I'm not confident.” The article says “last month” (it was 30 Sep) and paraphrases “dismiss mainstream stupidity” as “free thought”.

checks.what: His correction (8 Oct 2026): “I was wrong, I was publicly wrong, and the people who were most unjustly inconvenienced as a result were the RMN orgynizers.” He gives as his “median guess” that attendance has decided no one's job or status, says he is “still not confident”, and says the update came from an organizer of the events whom he is dating, after his funding was cancelled over the comment. open: Whether any account, report or case exists beyond this one incident, which three women say affected them.

How many attendees work in AI, and where: the article says it is “hard to know”, that filings “suggest” a “substantial” overlap, and, with no source given, “disproportionate”; the 30 Sep commenter later put the overlap with rationalists at “probably closer to 25% than 50%”. No count was found. The cofounder, before the article, put AI-lab attendees at “no more than 5? Out of a total of ~200”, none in roles building AI.
A New York Times piece of 21 Sep 2026 on an AI party house and networking could not be read (blocked); whether it bears on this is unchecked.
No Wikipedia article was found citing the story as of 18 Nov 2026.

Responses from OpenAI and the listed managers: none found by 18 Nov 2026. The cofounder's replies are under Responses. No correction from the Free Beacon (its page was modified seven hours after publication; what changed is not shown) or the New York Post, which ran a second article.
No Community Note on the reporter's post on X was seen through a mirror (18 Nov); X itself did not load.
cautions: The article says both that it is “hard to know” what share of attendees work in AI and, later and with no source given, that the parties “have been known to attract a disproportionate number of employees at Anthropic and OpenAI”. Relays carried the second sentence (see How it travelled).

The lede says he “runs a business”; the subhead and body say he is “listed as manager”. The filings name managers and do not say who runs the events. The lede's “allegations” rests, in the body, on “at least one woman”, whose account also describes the organizers acting on it.
Anthropic's response differs by outlet: the company “does not comment on individual employees” (Free Beacon) and “declined to comment” (New York Post).
India Today's kicker says the business is “facing sexual assault charges”; its own body says a woman “complained” and that the report does not accuse the employee. No source for any charge was found.

The women affected by the one incident the article rests on say the reporter did not contact them, that the organizers removed the man and offered to support them in going to the police, and that the article could have given their perspective.
The researcher the article quotes on careers publicly withdrew that view five weeks before it ran, on the word of an organizer he says he is dating; he calls it his median guess.
An employee's outside business is not the employer's act. No source found ties Anthropic or OpenAI as companies to the business.

travelled_summary: Scored by two coders who saw only the words, shuffled, without dates or outlets, under rules written down first. Across 24 statements (these 20 and four replies on X), hedges fell as the dates got later (Spearman −0.36) and attribution moved from “critics say” toward plain assertion and “the report found” (+0.53). Labels did not grow (+0.11): the 2023 pieces already used “sexual assault” and “abuse”. Agreement between coders was high (weighted kappa 0.97 and 1.00), but both were the same AI model, and the statements were gathered by people who expected the claim to harden.

It says CAIS “today joined a rare coalition of prominent figures in signing the MisAnthropic Statement” and quotes Hendrycks: “You cannot credibly claim to be safe while weakening your own previous safety commitments and asking the public for tens of billions of dollars to build recursively self-improving AI.” Its “Key Evidence”: that Anthropic warns of recursive self-improvement while “pitching recursive self-improvement to public-market investors as one of its core competitive advantages”; that in February it “weakened its Responsible Scaling Policy, including fully abandoning its unilateral commitments to pause”; and that it “has lobbied to weaken SB 1047, the RAISE Act, the AEGIS Act, and privately advocated for federal pre-emption of state AI laws.” The same release went out as a paid release on Business Wire.

responses.what: “AI that can build itself would be a major development in the history of technology—one that could bring enormous good for the world in science, healthcare, and beyond.” And: “In the coming months, we will organize conversations where policymakers, researchers, civil society, and other AI companies can help answer some of the questions this piece raises”.

open: Whether Anthropic replies, and whether any person listed says they did not sign. None found so far.

Whether the registration statement presents recursive self-improvement as a competitive strength, as the release says; and the RAISE Act, AEGIS Act and pre-emption claims, whose sources were not read.

Hendrycks, in a post on X seen only in a relay (Digg): “Numerous AI safety groups told us privately they agreed with this statement, yet felt unable to sign without risking relationships or future funding.” The groups are not named, and no way to check this was found.
cautions: This map is made with AI models made by Anthropic, the company the statement is about, on the day its shares are priced. A person independent of Anthropic should re-read these sources.
The statement itself gives no evidence; its grounds are in CAIS's press release, which is also a paid release on Business Wire.

The release says Anthropic was “fully abandoning its unilateral commitments to pause”. The RSP it cites drops the earlier unconditional commitment, by the company's own account, and keeps conditional commitments to delay (Appendix A).
The statement says the pledges were weakened “quietly”. The RSP change was announced in a post on Anthropic's site on 24 Feb 2026, with the reasons quoted under Responses.

The list is changing: 92 names when read at 18:17 UTC; one outlet's headline earlier gave 89. On the page, three names run together on one line (Joseph Jacks, Joe Allen, Dylan Hadfield-Menell). Titles are as the page lists them; a listed affiliation is not that institution's endorsement.
That some signatories lead or co-founded companies in the same market, and that CAIS's director signs, says who is speaking; it does not make the charge true or false.

Who pays: on the money view, several signatories' organisations (CAIS, ControlAI, PauseAI, the Midas Project, Encode, CHT) receive grants from Jaan Tallinn, from Dustin Moskovitz through SFF, or from FLI. Tallinn led Anthropic's 2021 Series A, in which Moskovitz also took part. This says who is speaking; it does not make the charge true or false.

title: A New Yorker feature on MAPLE, a Buddhist monastery in Vermont that works on AI, and the monastery's reply
standing: A magazine writer who visited the monastery and interviewed its head teacher, Soryu Forall. The piece ran under “Annals of Religion”.
claim: The Buddhist A.I. Sect That Wants to Take Over Silicon Valley. MAPLE promises to teach us how to live in the age of A.I. Its secret mission is much stranger.
source: The New Yorker, 16 Nov 2026 (headline and subheading, read on a screenshot of the page)
why: A monastery that says it is “designing a religion capable of correctly guiding AI systems”, reported on by a national magazine, with the monastery's public reply beside it.

checks.what: The feature itself was not read here. The New Yorker's site refuses the tools this project uses, and copies reposted on other sites were not used. A person needs to read it.
checks.source: The New Yorker

checks.what: The headline and subheading quoted above, on a screenshot of the article page in a reader's post on X, 17 Nov 2026. The address is the one MAPLE's reply links to.
checks.source: a post on X, 17 Nov 2026, seen in a screenshot

checks.what: What MAPLE says it does: “we are striving to care for life on Earth by designing a religion capable of correctly guiding AI systems.” Of the phrase the feature quotes from its website, “Designing Religion for the Age of A.I.”, MAPLE writes: “This is indeed what we believe, and what we are doing about it.”
checks.source: MAPLE's reply to the feature, on its own site (undated; online by 18 Nov 2026)

checks.what: On the “secret mission”: MAPLE writes that its secret doctrine “does exist, and it relates to the solution to the AI problem, not to the definition of the problem”, that it shares it only with people in its training, and that “we disagree with his characterization of our secret doctrine.”
checks.source: MAPLE's reply to the feature, on its own site (undated; online by 18 Nov 2026)

responses.who: MAPLE (the Monastic Academy for the Preservation of Life on Earth)
responses.what: says it wants to “correct some inaccuracies in the article”. “The article says that our main focus is to stop AI. It is not.” “We do not aim to stop AI, but to guide its development in such a way that it makes our society less destructive rather than more destructive.”
responses.source: MAPLE's reply to the feature, on its own site (undated; online by 18 Nov 2026)

responses.who: MAPLE
responses.what: “Does this mean we’re trying to build an AI guru, some kind of AI sage, a programmed messiah? The article says we are. However, we are not.”
responses.source: MAPLE's reply to the feature, on its own site (undated; online by 18 Nov 2026)

responses.who: MAPLE
responses.what: on its head teacher's childhood, which the feature recounts: he describes “overcoming the view that humanity “has to go”, or deserves to die, due to the destruction it has wrought on the natural world. We must emphasize that this is a view that Forall overcame as a teenager.”
responses.source: MAPLE's reply to the feature, on its own site (undated; online by 18 Nov 2026)

responses.who: MAPLE
responses.what: on residents not talking to the reporter: the community was “in noble silence” during the visit and chose “to have a chaperone in organized one-on-ones with Sam”.
responses.source: MAPLE's reply to the feature, on its own site (undated; online by 18 Nov 2026)

responses.who: MAPLE
responses.what: on a former resident the feature quotes (a private person, not named here): it calls his claims “not merely a mischaracterization but part of a deliberate project by a group that is competing with us to influence the ethics of AI systems”, and says “self-harm is not acceptable or part of spiritual practice.”
responses.source: MAPLE's reply to the feature, on its own site (undated; online by 18 Nov 2026)

responses.who: A trainee at MAPLE (a private person, not named here)
responses.what: published a reply to the former resident's account the day before the feature appeared. Not read here beyond its title and date.

open: The feature's own words on the “secret mission”, an AI guru, taking over Silicon Valley and the former resident's account. A person should read it and set it against MAPLE's reply, point by point.

Former residents have published their own accounts of life at MAPLE on LessWrong: an open letter (16 Dec 2021), a post on MAPLE and the wider community (19 Aug 2025) and a long account of “high-control dynamics” (29 Jul 2026). None has been read here yet, and the map draws nothing from them.
The interview recordings MAPLE links from its reply have not been listened to here.
cautions: “Sect” is the magazine's headline word, not this map's.

As MAPLE quotes it, the feature ends: “It’s a shame that MAPLE is so secretive about its secret doctrine, because, in a way, I think the group is closer to the truth than anyone else I’d encountered.” Those are the feature's words as MAPLE relays them, not read in the feature itself.

The former resident and the trainee are private persons and are named here by role only. Both the feature and MAPLE's reply name the former resident, who has also published his own account of MAPLE under his name; because he went public on this matter himself, both pages are linked.
MAPLE's reply mentions a self-harm account from the feature; this record does not repeat it. If you or someone you know is struggling, call or text 988 (the Suicide and Crisis Lifeline, US).
These records were made with AI models made by Anthropic. No source read here makes Anthropic a party to this matter.
